text: I read that the field course in week six is done in mixed groups together with the students from the partner programme, and I will be honest that this is the part I am least looking forward to. I grew up in a very small town and did all of my schooling with the same twenty people, so meeting an entirely new group is genuinely hard for me.

The first lecture covered central place theory, which I had never heard of before. I found the worked example with the market towns far easier to follow than the formal definition that came before it.
One thing I still do not understand is how we are supposed to compare two regions when they collect their census data in completely different ways?

We had the first joint seminar with the other group today. It was much less awkward than I had built it up to be. One of them had already read the book I was struggling with and explained the argument better than the lecture did.

I noticed that I kept waiting to be asked for my opinion, while the others simply offered theirs. I had assumed that was politeness on my part, and then realised it just looked like I had nothing to say. I started speaking earlier in the discussion after that.

The field week was the best part of the course by a long way. Working out a land-use survey with people who learned geography under a different curriculum meant we argued for an hour about what counted as urban before we could begin. That argument taught me more than the reading had.
Long week. Good though.

I have signed up for the semester abroad, which I would have called impossible back in September. I was hesitant at the very start of this course and I am now the person telling everyone else to choose the field option.
I am still a quiet person in groups and I do not think that part changes. What changed is that I stopped reading my own silence as a failure, and I now ask for the floor when I actually need it.

I signed up for this seminar mainly because it is taught jointly with the group at the partner institution, and I have wanted an excuse to work with people outside my own department for two years now. I come from a family where everyone talks over everyone else at dinner, so I am rarely the one who holds back in a discussion.
We spent the whole first session on abbreviation conventions in funerary inscriptions. I had not appreciated how much of the reading is reconstruction rather than transcription.
The joint sessions are timetabled at an hour that works for exactly one of the two groups, and it is not ours. Three people from our side have simply stopped coming and I do not blame them for it.
Our joint transcription came back with the comment that we had used two different citation styles throughout. That is because we never agreed on one, and nobody wanted to be the person who insisted.

I no longer think of the shared sessions as part of the seminar at all. We attend, we present, we leave. Whatever collaboration was supposed to happen is not happening, and at this point I would rather have the hour back.
The palaeography exercises are excellent, though. Being handed a photograph with no transcription and told to argue for a reading is the most useful thing I have done in this degree.
If the seminar runs again in this format I would not recommend it to anyone. The subject deserves better than a video link that drops out every ten minutes.

I should also say that I am impatient with people who take a long time to answer, and I know that is partly a habit from my own upbringing rather than a fair standard to hold anyone to. I probably read hesitation as disinterest when it was nothing of the kind.

I grew up between two languages and two sets of grandparents who disagreed about almost everything, so a studio group with people from four countries feels ordinary to me rather than daunting. I already know that the same building gets described completely differently depending on who is doing the describing.
The first assignment is a measured drawing of a facade of our own choosing. I badly underestimated how long that takes to do properly and will start earlier next time.

Our studio group divided the survey work by building rather than by task, which meant everyone had to learn the whole method instead of becoming the person who only ever draws sections. It was slower and much better.

I have always been someone who switches into a far more formal register the moment I am not speaking my first language, and it happens whether I intend it or not. People occasionally read it as coldness.

I learned that what I was taught to call a courtyard covers at least three different things depending on which tradition you were trained in. Having that pointed out by somebody trained differently was more useful than any glossary.
Studio was fine.
I would take this studio again and I have already told the second years to choose it. The mixed groups are the reason for that, not a side effect of it.
I am not a confident presenter and ten weeks has not changed that. But I noticed I was less anxious presenting to the mixed group than to my own cohort, which I had not expected at all.
I am not sure how the group project is supposed to work when half of us have done calculus before and half of us have not. Are we all going to be graded on the same output?

In my family nobody does anything alone, decisions very much included, and I bring that into group work whether it suits the task or not. I find people who prefer to split the work up and then disappear genuinely difficult to deal with.

The others were far better prepared than I had expected, which was a relief, but they had also settled the entire analysis plan in a chat I was not part of. I was annoyed for a day and then realised I had never actually asked to be added.
Bootstrapping finally made sense once I saw it done by hand on twenty rows. The lecture slides had made it look like a magic trick.
I was hesitant at first, I will say that plainly. Now the group is the only reason I have kept up at all, because somebody always notices when one of us has gone quiet.
Doing all of it online is the problem here, not the people. Text is a terrible medium for arguing about a model specification.
Useful course. Badly timetabled.
I have learned that I need to see somebody's face before I really trust their numbers, and that this says a great deal more about me than it does about them.

I am more excited about this ensemble than about anything else I am taking this term, mostly because of the visiting players. I was raised in a household where you did not contradict the person holding the baton, and then trained somewhere you were marked down for failing to argue with the conductor. I have spent years translating between those two instincts, so a rehearsal room full of people trained differently feels less like a problem and more like an ordinary Tuesday.
We are opening with a piece I have played before, which I had assumed would make the first rehearsal easy. It made it harder, because I had to unlearn a tempo I was attached to.

When the visiting cellist went quiet after my suggestion about the phrasing, my first assumption was that she disagreed with me. Where I trained, silence after a proposal means it is being taken seriously. I had to stop myself from explaining the same point three more times.
The rehearsal load was not shared fairly this block. Two of us prepared the difficult movement and four of us prepared the easy one, and I was one of the two.

The best moment so far was realising that the visiting violinist and I had been given contradictory instructions by our two teachers, and simply deciding between ourselves which one to follow. That felt like an ensemble rather than a timetabled activity.
I apologise before I ask a question. I have been told it makes me sound unsure of a reading I am actually quite confident about. It comes from home and I doubt it is going anywhere.
There was a real disagreement in week nine that we never resolved. One player stopped replying to messages and we performed without them. Nobody handled it well, and I include myself in that.

Looking back I was completely won over by the end, which surprises me because I began the term assuming the visiting players were a scheduling gimmick. What changed my mind was not a concert but a forty minute argument about a repeat.

I understand now that I hear directness as rudeness a good deal faster than the people I trained alongside do, and that this is something I brought into the room rather than anything anyone did to me.
